Q: Why does my query using "select distinct" and "where in" complete so slowly? A:

Assuming that this is your query:

select *
from table2 where row2_one in (select distinct row_one from table1 where row_two=5)

Then this is well-formed. One thing, you don't need the DISTINCT in the subquery.

If you add an index to the table1 on the column row_two, you should get better performance. An index on row2_one in table2 would also speed it up.

Q: Type narrowing fails when default destructured function argument is provided A:

This is a missing feature/bug in TypeScript, which was noted when control flow analysis for destructured function arguments was added and is described in an open issue on the TypeScript GitHub.

Thanks to @MattKantor for the relevant GitHub links added in a comment on a previous version of this question that had a bug in it.

Q: Is it possible to convert all higher-order logic and dependent type in Lean/Isabelle/Coq into first-order logic? A:

The short answer is: yes, it is not impractically large and this is done in particular when translating proofs to SMT solvers for sledgehammer-like tools. There is a fair amount of blowup, but it is a linear factor on the order of 2-5. You probably lose more from not having specific support for all the built in rules, and in the case of DTT, writing down all the defeq proofs which are normally implicit.

Q: How to web scrape sports team betting lines? A:

Yes, Selenium + BeautifulSoup can scrape it because the odds are rendered dynamically after the page loads.

You can also loop through each tr.firstline row and grab the values directly from the td classes. Something like this should work for most sportsbook tables:

for tr in soup.find_all('tr', {'class': 'firstline'}):
    team = tr.find('td', {'class': 'col_teamname'}).text.strip()
    spread = tr.find_all('td', {'class': 'hdcp'})[0].text.strip()
    total = tr.find_all('td', {'class': 'hdcp'})[1].text.strip()
    moneyline = tr.find('td', {'class': 'moneylineodds'}).text.strip()
    start_time = tr.find('td', {'class': 'col_time'}).text.strip()

    print(team, spread, total, moneyline, start_time)

One thing to watch out for is sportsbooks changing class names or rendering odds through APIs/websockets later on. Sometimes using the site's network requests is easier than scraping HTML directly.

I learned a lot of the sports odds structure stuff from reading different sports betting data discussions and odds comparison articles on sports betting lines too.

Q: Off-by-one when counting words in dictionary A:

According to the specification, none of the words in this dictionary are longer than 45.

You must account for the Line Feed, as well as the NUL added by fgets. If the largest word has 45 characters, your buffer must have space for 47.

The dictionary does indeed contain a line with a 45-character word:

         1         2         3         4     4
1234567890123456789012345678901234567890123456
pneumonoultramicroscopicsilicovolcanoconiosis␊

Including the line feed, that line contains 46 characters.

fgets places the first 44 and a NUL in word in one pass, then the last character of the word, the LF and a NUL in the next pass. So that line increases the count by two.

Increase the buffer size to 47 (or use an approach that doesn't require knowing the maximum word length in advance).

Q: Can I use Visual Studio Code to create/publish SSIS packages? A:

No, you cannot use Visual Studio Code to create SSIS packages, but you also do not need Visual Studio Professional. You can use SQL Server Data Tools, which you can install during your Visual Studio installation or install with the stand-alone installer.

If you are only doing T-SQL and SSIS development, then you probably don't need Visual Studio Professional. I don't think there is anything SSDT is missing regarding SSIS development. Saying that, I currently use Professional, but I used to use just SSDT, and I never ran into any limitations concerning SSIS development.

Q: The difference between a 'closure' and a 'lambda' A:

I have tried to read previous answers and comments, and I am surprised about the wording needed for just a simple concept.

Lambda applied to a set will always return the same result.

A closure applied to a set may change the return result over time as it uses dynamic parameters, so to speak, that may change over time.

Lambda in simple terms (ignoring the "anonymous" condition):

var c = 1
int lambda(a, b) = a + b
lambda(1, 2) = 3
c = 2
lambda(1, 2) = 3

A closure in simple terms

var c = 1
int closure(a, b) = a + b + c
closure(1, 2) = 4
c = 2
closure(1, 2) = 5
